final_proof:
Let the sum of a family of nonnegative real numbers be understood in the usual unordered sense
\[
 \sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\sup\left\{\sum_{i\in F}a_i:F\subseteq I\text{ finite}\right\}.
\]
Thus the Hilbert direct sum is
\[
 H=\left\{x=(x_i)_{i\in I}:x_i\in H_i\text{ and }
       \sum_{i\in I}\|x_i\|_{H_i}^{\,2}<\infty\right\}.
\]
It is a vector space: for example,
\(
\|x_i+y_i\|^2\le 2\|x_i\|^2+2\|y_i\|^2
\)
for every \(i\), so \(x+y\in H\) whenever \(x,y\in H\); closure under scalar multiplication is immediate.

For \(x,y\in H\), define
\[
 \langle x,y\rangle_H:=\sum_{i\in I}\langle x_i,y_i\rangle_{H_i}.
\]
This unordered sum is well-defined and absolutely convergent. Indeed, for every finite \(F\subseteq I\), the finite-dimensional Cauchy--Schwarz inequality for real numbers gives
\[
 \sum_{i\in F}\bigl|\langle x_i,y_i\rangle_{H_i}\bigr|
 \le \sum_{i\in F}\|x_i\|\,\|y_i\|
 \le
 \left(\sum_{i\in F}\|x_i\|^2\right)^{1/2}
 \left(\sum_{i\in F}\|y_i\|^2\right)^{1/2}
 \le \|x\|_2\|y\|_2,
\]
where \(\|x\|_2=(\sum_i\|x_i\|^2)^{1/2}\). Hence the family of scalar summands is absolutely summable. (Equivalently, only countably many of its terms are nonzero, and the resulting series converges absolutely.) Consequently sums may be added and scalar multiples may be taken term by term. The inner-product axioms therefore follow from those in each \(H_i\). Moreover,
\[
 \langle x,x\rangle_H=\sum_{i\in I}\|x_i\|_{H_i}^{\,2}=\|x\|_2^2,
\]
and if this is zero, every \(x_i\) is zero. Thus \(H\) is an inner-product space, with the indicated norm.

It remains to prove completeness. Let \((x^{(n)})_{n\ge1}\) be Cauchy in \(H\), writing \(x^{(n)}=(x_i^{(n)})_{i\in I}\). For each fixed \(i\),
\[
 \|x_i^{(n)}-x_i^{(m)}\|_{H_i}
 \le \|x^{(n)}-x^{(m)}\|_2,
\]
so \((x_i^{(n)})_n\) is Cauchy in the complete space \(H_i\). Let
\(x_i=\lim_{n\to\infty}x_i^{(n)}\) and put \(x=(x_i)_{i\in I}\).

Every Cauchy sequence is bounded, so choose \(M<\infty\) such that \(\|x^{(n)}\|_2\le M\) for all \(n\). If \(F\subseteq I\) is finite, coordinatewise convergence and continuity of the norm give
\[
 \sum_{i\in F}\|x_i\|^2
   =\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{i\in F}\|x_i^{(n)}\|^2
   \le M^2.
\]
Taking the supremum over all finite \(F\) shows that \(\sum_i\|x_i\|^2\le M^2\), hence \(x\in H\).

Finally, let \(\varepsilon>0\). Choose \(N\) such that
\(\|x^{(n)}-x^{(m)}\|_2<\varepsilon\) whenever \(n,m\ge N\). Fix \(n\ge N\). For every finite \(F\subseteq I\), letting \(m\to\infty\) in the finite sum yields
\[
 \sum_{i\in F}\|x_i^{(n)}-x_i\|^2
 =\lim_{m\to\infty}\sum_{i\in F}
       \|x_i^{(n)}-x_i^{(m)}\|^2
 \le \varepsilon^2.
\]
Taking the supremum over finite \(F\) gives
\(\|x^{(n)}-x\|_2\le\varepsilon\). Therefore \(x^{(n)}\to x\) in \(H\). Every Cauchy sequence in \(H\) converges, so \(H\) is complete and hence is a Hilbert space.
